title: State v. Devon Marsh
summary: A rare 19th-century watch vanished from the Hallstrom Gallery the night before its biggest auction. Devon Marsh, the gallery's late-shift security guard, is the only person whose badge opened the display case that night.
prosecutionStatement: One badge opened that case at **2:14 in the morning**. It was not a curator's. It was not a cleaner's. It belonged to the man paid to guard it. Add $9,000 of debt and a watch worth two hundred times that, and the picture is **not complicated**.
defenseStatement: Three other people held that override code. *Three.* And 6 minutes after the scan the State keeps waving at you, Devon Marsh filed the report that told everyone the case was open. _Think about that._ **Thieves do not report their own thefts.**

evidence.title: Badge access log
evidence.description: Marsh's badge opened the display case at 2:14 a.m., forty minutes into his shift.

evidence.title: Debt records
evidence.description: Marsh owed a collections agency roughly $9,000 at the time of the theft.

evidence.title: Override code list
evidence.description: Three other staff members had the case's override code active that week.

evidence.title: Marsh's incident report
evidence.description: Marsh filed a report about the open case at 2:20 a.m. — six minutes after the badge scan, before the gallery even opened the next day.

evidence.title: Curator's calendar
evidence.description: The curator had scheduled unrelated after-hours case maintenance that same night but never logged it.

evidence.title: Pawn shop tip
evidence.description: A note passed to you before the trial: someone tried to sell a watch matching the description two towns over, three days after the theft — using a name that isn't Marsh's.
